name: The Replacements
label: Twin/Tone
lede: Two brothers who couldn't play well enough to quit, a janitor with a notebook, and a decade of finding the most reliable way to wreck a good night.

eras.title: Dogbreath in a basement
eras.text: Two brothers, a drummer and a janitor with a notebook. They start out as a cover band with no singer and end up with a name they took after getting banned from a church hall.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Tommy Stinson
years.h: Bob Stinson hands his kid brother a bass. The band is called Dogbreath
years.p: [[Bob Stinson|49771251-1082-4a3d-b48f-ba39e3be4a2b]] hands his eleven-year-old brother [[Tommy Stinson|3182bda5-2f4a-49e4-9fa3-cf7e5ebbff24]] a bass and recruits drummer [[Chris Mars|b0fefe3c-b393-4498-9b33-255b02d75716]]. They cover Aerosmith, Ted Nugent and Yes, with no singer.
years.xp:
Wikipedia puts the band's formation at 1979 but dates its beginnings to 1978, when Bob Stinson gave Tommy the bass. The trio rehearsed in the Stinson family house in south Minneapolis.

The name was Dogbreath, and the set was arena rock. There was nobody out front, which is about to change.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · St. Louis Magazine
years.h: [[Paul Westerberg|d558f844-4db0-4bc3-ba22-49ad2ca2722e]], a janitor, hears them through the wall and joins
years.p: Westerberg is cleaning U.S. Senator David Durenberger's office when he hears the Stinsons rehearsing. Mars invites him to jam, and he ends up replacing the singer.
years.xp:
According to Wikipedia, Westerberg got the job by telling the outgoing vocalist "The band doesn't like you."

St. Louis Magazine, summarizing Bob Mehr's biography Trouble Boys, says the band came to the janitor as high school dropouts and that Bob would punch Tommy in the face when he made mistakes.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Twin/Tone Records
years.h: Westerberg hands a four-song basement demo to a record store clerk
years.p: [[Peter Jesperson|00cefb4a-65c2-4faa-812a-8f182b5bc8e9]] runs the Oar Folkjokeopus record store and co-runs Twin/Tone Records. He plays the tape at the counter and signs the band to Twin/Tone that year.
years.xp:
Jesperson later described the moment: "I didn't even get through the first song before I thought my head was going to explode."

Twin/Tone had been founded in 1977 by Jesperson, Charley Hallman and Paul Stark. It ended up releasing more than 300 records before closing in 1994.

years.h: The Impediments get banned from a church hall and become the Replacements
years.p: Playing a gig without Tommy, the band was thrown out for disorderly conduct after a drunken show. Wikipedia says the ban is what led them to rename themselves.
years.xp:
The band had just discovered the Clash and the Damned and dropped the Dogbreath repertoire. They had renamed themselves the Impediments, and were banned under that name.

The story is told the same way in most retellings, and Wikipedia is the source used here.

years.cap: American rock band The Replacements in a 1984 publicity photo taken by Laura... · Wikimedia
years.h: First show as the Replacements: Jay's Longhorn, Minneapolis
years.p: The band plays its first gig under the new name at Jay's Longhorn, a Minneapolis punk bar. Westerberg is the frontman, the Stinsons are still teenagers, and there is nothing else on the record yet.

eras.title: Fast, loud and out of tune
eras.text: Sorry Ma, Stink and Hootenanny come out on Twin/Tone, and the band learns that its best songs are the slow ones. It also learns that it is very good at getting thrown out of places.

years.h: Sorry Ma, Forgot to Take Out the Trash on Twin/Tone
years.p: Recorded in July 1980 and again from March to June 1981, released August 25. The first single, "I'm in Trouble," came out August 7.
years.xp:
Westerberg, Jesperson and Steve Fjelstad produced. "Somethin to Dü" is the band's nod to fellow Twin Cities punks [[Hüsker Dü|5c4c90a4-539f-4101-83cf-301bc6a94e06]].

Robert Christgau gave it a B+ in the Village Voice. AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine later called it one of the best LPs the whole scene produced in the early '80s.
play: Sorry Ma, Forgot to Take Out the Trash

years.h: Stink: eight songs, fourteen minutes
years.p: Recorded at Blackberry Way in one session on March 13, released June 24. It opens with "Kids Don't Follow," over a recording of police breaking up a rent party.
years.xp:
The audio comes from a January 29, 1982 raid on a rent party at the Harmony Building in Minneapolis. The EP runs 14 minutes 24 seconds.

Jesperson and Fjelstad produced. Wikipedia describes it as the band's hardcore punk attempt.

years.h: Hootenanny: Westerberg plays everything on one song
years.p: Released April 29. "Within Your Reach" is Westerberg alone; on the title track Mars plays lead guitar and Bob Stinson plays bass.
years.xp:
Recording ran from October 1982 to January 1983, mostly at the Stark/Mudge Mobile Unit warehouse in Brooklyn Center, with sessions at Blackberry Way and a basement.

"Lovelines" takes its words from the City Pages classifieds, and the cover was drawn by Hüsker Dü's [[Grant Hart|571e1aad-0512-45ec-a26d-1d09d786cc53]], credited as Fake Name Graphx. Wikipedia reports over 38,000 vinyl copies sold.

years.h: First U.S. tour: Tommy Stinson drops out of tenth grade to go
years.p: The band hits the road in April 1983 with a roadie named Bill Sullivan. Tommy is a tenth-grader when he leaves school for it.

years.h: CBGB: Bob is thrown out on arrival, the band plays last of five bands
years.p: The band reaches New York in June 1983. Bob Stinson is thrown out of CBGB when they arrive and they play early Monday morning to a room that has mostly left.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says shows at CBGB and Folk City that trip did badly because the band was so loud.

Later that summer they opened eight dates for R.E.M. Per the same account, the band decided to alienate the audience and several members threatened to quit.

eras.title: The one everyone points to
eras.text: Let It Be arrives in 1984 and does what none of the earlier records could: it makes the case that Westerberg can write. Sire is watching, and the band is doing its best to give them reasons not to sign.

years.cap: The cover photo, by Daniel Corrigan, was taken on the roof of the Stinsons' mother's house.
years.src: Wikipedia: Let It Be · Wikipedia: The Replacements (band)
years.h: Let It Be: the roof of the Stinsons' mother's house
years.p: Recorded at Blackberry Way from August 1983 to February 1984 and released October 2. Robert Christgau gave it an A+.
years.xp:
Westerberg said "playing that kind of noisy, fake hardcore rock was getting us nowhere," and called it the first time he had songs the band arranged.

[[Peter Buck|2bab20bf-8dab-4af8-b7b0-ba8e30860261]] of R.E.M. was rumored to be producing. He says he did pre-production, one solo (on "I Will Dare"), and gave them some ideas. Steve Fjelstad and Jesperson produced.

Rolling Stone later ranked it #15 among the albums of the 1980s. The current owners of the roof house added a stained-glass window of the cover photo in 2019.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: For Sale
years.h: The Shit Hits the Fans: a live tape of the band at its loosest
years.p: The cassette is the band's only live release for decades, with false starts and stops throughout. Wikipedia describes it as an example of the intentionally poor shows label reps got to see.
years.xp:
By 1985 several major labels were interested. Wikipedia says the band was broke and Bob Stinson was working as a pizza chef.

Tommy Stinson said in 2007 that there were no good Replacements live recordings.

years.h: Tim: the Sire debut, produced by Tommy Ramone
years.p: Recorded June to July 1985 at Nicollet Studios, released September 18 per Wikipedia. Tommy Erdelyi, the original Ramones drummer, produced.
years.xp:
Sire's Seymour Stein signed the band; he had managed the Ramones. The "Bastards of Young" video is a single shot of a speaker.

Wikipedia lists the peak at #183 on the Billboard 200. Rolling Stone's review said the record's swagger and unpolished reflection became a template for grunge, alt-country and later emo.

The band page on Wikipedia dates the release to October 1985, and the album page to September 18. See questions.

eras.title: Sire, Saturday Night Live and the last Bob show
eras.text: Six months on a major label produce the most famous bad night on television, a Hoboken set Sire tried to bottle, and the end of the original band.

years.cap: American rock band The Replacements in a publicity photo, dated circa 1983,... · Wikimedia
years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · St. Louis Magazine
years.h: Saturday Night Live: they show up drunk and get banned
years.p: Last-minute guests, they play "Bastards of Young" out of tune, then return wearing each other's clothes for "Kiss Me on the Bus." Lorne Michaels bans them.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says [[G.E. Smith|a289a494-cd2d-458b-91b8-f161dd467626]], SNL's music director and a fan, arranged the booking. He told the story that crew members had smuggled liquor into the dressing room and Bob Stinson fell in the corridor and broke his guitar, so SNL lent him one.

Wikipedia also notes Westerberg is heard swearing off-microphone at Bob. Per Trouble Boys, as summarized by St. Louis Magazine, Michaels said they would never work in television again. Westerberg came back as a solo act in 1993.

yt: Bastards of Young, live at Maxwell's 1986
years.h: Maxwell's, Hoboken: Sire brings a mobile studio
years.p: Seymour Stein books a mobile unit to record the show as a marketing tool. It sits in the can for 31 years.
years.xp:
For Sale: Live at Maxwell's 1986 came out on Rhino on October 6, 2017, produced by Bob Mehr. It reached #52 on the Billboard 200, and Pitchfork gave it an 8.7.

Wikipedia notes it captures the band months before Bob Stinson was gone.

years.src: Wikipedia: Bob Stinson · Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Life of the Record
years.h: Bob Stinson leaves the band he founded
years.p: Wikipedia says he was fired or chose to leave, or both, over creative and personal differences and his drinking and drug use. Westerberg said he ran out of ideas that Bob could shine on.
years.xp:
Bob Stinson's Wikipedia page says he was forced out in summer 1986 and that the band later reframed it as growing up. Westerberg is quoted: "we drank and took drugs a lot... But Bob thought that was the Replacements." The band page dates it to August 1986; Tommy Stinson's page says 1985. See questions.

Manager Peter Jesperson was fired the same year. He said it was like being thrown out of a club he had helped start.

Life of the Record has Westerberg saying they were thinking of breaking up the band when they let Bob go, and instead kept the trio.

eras.title: Three guys and a janitor
eras.text: Memphis, a new guitarist, two attempts at radio and one record that was mostly Westerberg. It ends in a Chicago park with the roadies on stage.

years.src: Wikipedia: Pleased to Meet Me · Life of the Record
years.h: Pleased to Meet Me, recorded in Memphis without Bob
years.p: Recorded at Ardent Studios from November 1986 to January 1987 with producer Jim Dickinson. It is the only Replacements studio album made as a trio.
years.xp:
Westerberg met Chilton at a 1984 CBGB show, per Life of the Record, and the song grew from that awkward first meeting. Bob Stinson turned up for one session. Dickinson's joke working title was "Where's Bob?" Alex Chilton and the Memphis Horns played on it.

Luther Dickinson recalls his father putting a toxic waste barrel in front of Mars's kick drum for a "polluted sound." Westerberg said going to Memphis was the coolest thing they ever did.

It placed third in the Village Voice's 1987 Pazz & Jop poll.

years.src: Life of the Record · Wikipedia: Pleased to Meet Me
years.h: Warner Bros. throws a playback party and picks up the option
years.p: Warner flies 30 to 40 industry people to Memphis to hear Pleased to Meet Me and exercises the band's contract option on the spot.
years.xp:
Bob Mehr says that was Westerberg's answer to the label. Life of the Record reports the album about doubled Tim's sales, to roughly 250,000 copies, which was a disappointment at the time.

The Wikipedia album page cites journalist Michael Azerrad for about 300,000. See questions.

years.h: Slim Dunlap, First Avenue's janitor, takes the guitar job
years.p: [[Slim Dunlap|0e10e22b-2a2f-48f8-b54f-cc1523312dce]] turns Westerberg down at first. He joins in 1987 out of admiration for the songs and stays until the end.
years.xp:
He was working as a janitor at First Avenue, the club where the band started. Wikipedia quotes him preferring to "just play guitar and let the other guy lose all the money."

His first solo record, The Old New Me, came out in 1993, made for under $10,000.

years.h: Don't Tell a Soul: the band goes for radio
years.p: Released February 1 on Sire. Recorded at Cherokee Studios in Hollywood with producer Matt Wallace and mixed by Chris Lord-Alge. "I'll Be You" is their only Hot 100 entry, at #51.
years.xp:
Westerberg was not sold on the polish: "I thought the little things I'd cut in my basement were closer to what I wanted."

"I'll Be You" hit #51 on May 13, 1989 and also topped the Modern Rock chart. Wallace's remix of the album came out in 2019 as Dead Man's Pop.

years.h: All Shook Down: a Westerberg solo album with the name on it
years.p: It began as a solo record, and management talked him into releasing it as the Replacements. John Cale plays viola on "Sadly Beautiful" and Johnette Napolitano sings on "My Little Problem."
years.xp:
Wikipedia notes there are no clear records of who played on which tracks. Rolling Stone ranked it third among its 1990 albums of the year.

Chris Mars left in November 1990, and his last appearance as a Replacement was in the "Merry Go Round" video. Steve Foley replaced him for the tour.

years.h: Chris Mars quits; Steve Foley plays the last tour
years.p: Mars, drummer since the Dogbreath days, is out after All Shook Down. Foley drums the final six months.

years.h: The last show for 22 years: the roadies play the encore
years.p: At Taste of Chicago, with Material Issue, each band member wanders off during the set and a roadie takes his place. Fans call it "It Ain't Over 'Til the Fat Roadie Plays."
years.xp:
WXRT in Chicago broadcast the show live. It was the last time the band played until Riot Fest in 2013.

Their last tour, with Elvis Costello, had ended at Madison Square Garden in June. Wikipedia describes the band as having disbanded in 1991.

eras.title: What happened to everybody
eras.text: The Replacements are gone but the records keep getting reissued, and the people are not all okay. Bob Stinson dies, Tommy Stinson ends up in Guns N' Roses, and Slim Dunlap gets sick.

years.h: Bob Stinson dies at 35
years.p: He was found in his Uptown Minneapolis apartment. The Hennepin County medical examiner's report, two weeks later, gave the cause as organ failure from years of drug and alcohol abuse.
years.xp:
Early press speculated overdose or bad heroin; a syringe was found next to him. Wikipedia and Bob Mehr both report the medical examiner ruled that out. An assistant medical examiner said, "There is such a thing as total body failure."

His mother Anita bought a park bench near the Lake of the Isles in Minneapolis in his memory. Recordings from his last band, the Bleeding Hearts, came out in 2022 as Riches to Rags.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Tommy Stinson
years.h: Tommy Stinson joins Guns N' Roses
years.p: After [[Bash & Pop|c44092a6-d6be-4bfa-9650-edccc69f7a2b]] and Perfect, Tommy Stinson replaces Duff McKagan in [[Guns N' Roses|eeb1195b-f213-4ce1-b28c-8565211f8e43]] in 1998. He stays until McKagan comes back; Wikipedia says he joined at 31 on drummer Josh Freese's recommendation.
years.xp:
He also toured and recorded with [[Soul Asylum|b10db9ad-b4c3-47f3-a7a4-37864b134f65]] from 2005 to 2011 and put out solo records, Village Gorilla Head in 2004 and One Man Mutiny in 2011.

Westerberg released Folker in 2004, a return to melodic lo-fi, and Chris Mars settled into a career as a visual artist.

years.h: Rhino compilation adds two new songs with Josh Freese on drums
years.p: Don't You Know Who I Think I Was? pairs Twin/Tone and Sire tracks with "Pool & Dive" and "Message to the Boys," cut by Westerberg, Stinson and Mars at Flowers Studio in Minneapolis.
years.xp:
Rhino followed with deluxe editions of the four Twin/Tone albums on April 22, 2008 and the Sire albums on September 24, 2008.

That is not a reunion. Wikipedia lists it as a one-off session.

years.h: Steve Foley, the final drummer, dies
years.p: Wikipedia reports that Foley died from an accidental overdose of prescription medication.

years.src: Wikipedia: The Replacements (band) · Wikipedia: Slim Dunlap · Wikipedia: Peter Jesperson
years.h: Slim Dunlap suffers a stroke; friends start Songs for Slim
years.p: Wikipedia says Dunlap had a severe stroke in February 2012. Peter Jesperson organizes Songs for Slim, and Westerberg and Tommy Stinson record a 10-inch for it.
years.xp:
The Songs for Slim EP, in a 250-copy vinyl edition, was auctioned online for Dunlap's medical costs. Jesperson's Wikipedia page calls it the closest thing yet to a Replacements reunion.

A live album, Thank You Dancers!, followed in 2020.

years.src: Slicing Up Eyeballs · Wikipedia: The Replacements
years.h: Color Me Obsessed tells the band through its fans
years.p: Gorman Bechard's documentary has almost no Replacements playing on screen: the story comes from fans. Noisey and Vice streamed it on YouTube in December.
years.xp: Slicing Up Eyeballs described it as a two-hour documentary about the Replacements and their rabid fans, streamed for a limited time.

eras.title: The reunion
eras.text: Twenty-two years after Grant Park, Westerberg and Tommy Stinson come back with Dave Minehan on guitar and Josh Freese on drums. Three summers later, they are done.

years.h: Riot Fest Toronto: first show in 22 years
years.p: A 23-song, 75-minute set at Fort York, with Dave Minehan on guitar and Josh Freese on drums. Rolling Stone says nearly 10,000 people rushed the stage for "Can't Hardly Wait."
years.xp:
Westerberg opened by apologizing that it took so long, and said they had been having a wardrobe debate that was unresolved. He forgot some words and the crowd filled them in.

The set opened with the first track from Sorry Ma and ended on a song inspired by an Iggy Pop autograph. More Riot Fest dates followed in Chicago and Denver.

years.h: Coachella: Billie Joe Armstrong sits in on the second weekend
years.p: The Replacements play two sets at Coachella, April 11 and 18, and [[Billie Joe Armstrong|5d06fe54-485a-4a07-b506-5f6f719448cb]] of Green Day joins on the second date.

years.h: The Tonight Show: "Alex Chilton"
years.p: Twenty-eight years after being banned from Saturday Night Live, the band plays network television again, this time on The Tonight Show.

years.big: "I have always loved you. Now I must whore my past."
q: I have always loved you. Now I must whore my past.
years.h: Primavera Sound, Porto: Westerberg says it's the last show
years.p: At Primavera Sound in Porto, days after a Spain date, Westerberg announces on stage that this is the band's final performance. The T-shirts said it first.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says the message was split over two shirts, one letter on each side. In February 2015 co-manager Darren Hill said the band had laid down seven or eight songs for a possible album.

Tommy Stinson said that September they had dipped their toe in the water, and it did not feel so good.

eras.title: The reissues
eras.text: The band is done, the archive is not. A biography lays out the full story, and the back catalog gets the treatment it always deserved.

years.h: Bob Mehr's Trouble Boys tells the whole story
years.p: Mehr's biography, with band access, documents the Stinson brothers, the drinking, Bob's death from organ failure, and the way the group sabotaged its own shot at fame.
years.xp:
In a March 2016 NPR interview, Mehr described them as legends who never quite became stars.

He also produced the live Maxwell's album.

years.h: Slim Dunlap dies at 73
years.p: His family said the cause was complications from the 2012 stroke. He died at his Minneapolis home.
